chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Kazzaz, from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him).

Regarding a man who married a woman and found her to be leprous or hunchbacked: He said, if he had not yet entered into her (consummated the marriage) and had not yet specified (whether he would keep her or divorce her), then if he wishes he may divorce her, and if he wishes he may keep her, and she has no dowry. And if he enters into her, then she is his wife. This does not contradict the report we previously mentioned, that one of this type is returned without divorce, because his saying 'if he wishes he may divorce' is construed to mean 'if he wishes he may let her go,' because that is derived from the root of the language from the word 'divorce,' and it is not construed to mean the legal divorce due to the indication of the first report. As for his saying 'and if he enters into her, then she is his wife,' the way to understand this is to construe it to mean that if he enters into her with knowledge of her condition, then that is consent to her. And whenever he did not know that and entered into her, he has the right to return her, and she has the dowry for what he made permissible of her private part, according to what the earlier reports contained, and this is also confirmed.
ai.seo_question: What are the rights and options for a husband who discovers a physical defect in his wife after marriage?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies the linguistic nuance of the phrase 'if he wishes, he divorces' (in shi'a tallaqa), interpreting it as a right of retention rather than a mandatory divorce, thereby allowing the husband to keep the wife without a formal talaq if he accepts the defect. This ruling distinguishes between pre-consummation, where no dowry is due if he chooses to release her, and post-consummation, where the wife is entitled to the full dowry (sadaq) for what he made lawful of her body if the defect was unknown. The text emphasizes that this 'return' (rad) is distinct from 'divorce' (talaq), preserving the marital bond's integrity while addressing the defect.
